lesson.title: Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and the End of the War
lesson.summary: In August 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, bringing about Japan's surrender and ending World War II, a decision whose necessity historians still debate.
lesson.body:
By the summer of 1945, the island hopping campaign across the Pacific had brought American forces to Japan's doorstep, but at a staggering cost in lives at battles like Iwo Jima and Okinawa. American military planners were preparing for a full invasion of the Japanese home islands, codenamed Operation Downfall, and projected that it could produce casualties on a scale far beyond anything seen so far in the Pacific war, based on the ferocity of Japanese resistance in the island campaigns. At the same time, the Manhattan Project had just produced a working atomic bomb, tested successfully at Trinity in July 1945, giving President Harry Truman, who had become president after Roosevelt's death in April 1945, a new and terrible option.

On August 6, 1945, a U.S. B-29 bomber named the Enola Gay dropped an atomic bomb nicknamed Little Boy on the city of Hiroshima. Three days later, on August 9, 1945, a second bomb, nicknamed Fat Man, was dropped from a B-29 called Bockscar on the city of Nagasaki. Commonly cited estimates suggest that roughly seventy thousand to well over one hundred thousand people died in Hiroshima by the end of 1945, counting both the immediate blast and deaths from injuries and radiation in the following months, with tens of thousands more dying in Nagasaki; because records were incomplete and many deaths from radiation exposure occurred over time, historians generally describe these figures as estimated ranges rather than precise counts.

Japan announced its surrender on August 15, 1945, just days after the second bombing and after the Soviet Union had also declared war on Japan and invaded Japanese-held Manchuria on August 8. The formal surrender ceremony took place on September 2, 1945, aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, bringing World War II to its final close.

Historians continue to debate whether the atomic bombings were necessary to end the war. Some argue that the bombs, however terrible, likely saved lives overall by making a full invasion of Japan unnecessary, given how costly the fighting for much smaller islands like Iwo Jima and Okinawa had already proven. Others point to evidence that Japan's leadership was already exploring ways to end the war, especially after the Soviet declaration of war removed Japan's hopes of a negotiated peace brokered through Moscow, and argue that the bombings targeted civilian populations in ways that raise serious moral questions regardless of their military effect. This remains one of the most debated decisions of the entire war, without a single settled answer among historians.
